summary: Frank Liu of the Voyage AI team, now part of MongoDB, presents an overview of AI-powered search and retrieval at the AI Engineer World's Fair. He defines AI search as systems that find related concepts even without identical wording, understand user intent, and can perform reasoning and instruction following—going beyond traditional approaches like TF-IDF or BM25. He notes that 95 to 99 percent of systems he has seen use embeddings in some form, making embedding quality a core component. After a brief refresher on RAG and embeddings, Liu discusses three real-world applications, each with a lesson. First, chatting with codebases (continue.dev, open source) demonstrates that there is no one-size-fits-all embedding model or LLM; evaluation is essential, and Continue.dev found Voyage Code 3 performed best for code documentation and developer queries. Second, a domain-specific application highlights that embeddings alone are insufficient; structured data and filtering (e.g., legal documents filtered by state or document type) are often necessary and typically done in the vector store. Third, agentic retrieval involves feedback loops where the LLM may expand or decompose queries—for example, splitting a request for X's 2024 earnings into four quarterly queries sent to separate vector stores. Liu calls 2025 and possibly 2026 the year of agents, emphasizing the need for powerful conversational search systems. Looking to the future, he identifies three key directions: multimodality, exemplified by Voyage Multimodal 3 which embeds text, images, or interleaved text-plus-images into a single semantic space; instruction tuning and reasoning becoming part of embedding models, enabling users to steer vectors in particular directions by providing instructions alongside queries, such as asking the model to find documents that dive into detail about a specific aspect; and the agent-native database, where Voyage joining MongoDB consolidates multiple components—embedding, reranking, query augmentation, and decomposition—into a single data platform, replacing the complex multi-component setups common today. Liu suggests this consolidation will emerge more in the coming year and next, then opens the floor for questions.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Voyage AI Overview
sections.summary: Frank Liu introduces himself as part of the Voyage AI team, which joined MongoDB approximately three to four months prior. Voyage AI builds embedding models and rerankers for RAG and semantic search, available via API, Azure, and AWS marketplaces, now part of MongoDB. He frames the talk as a higher-level discussion of AI search.

sections.title: AI Search Definition and Embeddings Refresher
sections.summary: Liu defines AI-powered search as systems that find related concepts without identical wording, understand user intent, and perform reasoning and instruction following, going beyond BM25/TF-IDF. He reviews RAG and notes that 95 to 99 percent of systems he has seen use embeddings, making embedding quality a core component.

sections.title: Real-World Applications and Lessons
sections.summary: Three applications are discussed. First, continue.dev's codebase chat (RAG plus reranking) teaches that no one-size-fits-all embedding model or LLM exists; evaluation is essential, and Voyage Code 3 performed best. Second, a domain-specific application shows embeddings alone are insufficient; structured data and filtering in the vector store are needed. Third, agentic retrieval uses feedback loops with query expansion and decomposition, critical for the coming era of agents.

sections.title: Future Directions: Multimodality and Instruction Tuning
sections.summary: Liu identifies the future as 100% multimodal, with embedding models handling text, images, and audio together, demonstrated by Voyage Multimodal 3. He also predicts instruction tuning and reasoning will become part of embedding models, enabling users to steer vectors in particular directions by providing instructions alongside queries, such as asking the model to find documents that only dive into detail about a specific aspect.

sections.title: Agent-Native Database and Wrap-up
sections.summary: Liu introduces the agent-native database concept, enabled by Voyage joining MongoDB. He envisions consolidating the many components of search and retrieval—embedding, reranking, query augmentation, and query decomposition—into a single data platform, replacing complex multi-component setups. He suggests this will emerge more in the coming year and next, then opens the floor for questions and shares QR codes for following MongoDB/Voyage AI.
